extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and ethical standards for reviewing submissions to SIGGRAPH 2026 Technical Papers (dual-track and journal), covering evaluation criteria, review conduct, conflicts, anonymity, and procedural requirements. Intended to guide reviewers in deciding acceptance, track placement, and writing high-quality reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track suitability (Journal vs Conference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation on whether a submission is suitable for the Journal (ACM TOG) or Conference track; Journal papers are expected to satisfy ACM TOG criteria of excellence, present original, well validated, and comprehensively described research; Conference papers present original research but may have less comprehensive evidence/validation and are subject to length caps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide first whether the paper's overall contribution merits acceptance to the SIGGRAPH Technical Papers program; if positive, then evaluate completeness to determine track. For dual-track submissions, reviewers can recommend Journal or Conference, but the final decision is by the Technical Papers committee. Uniformly strong scores for a dual-track submission indicate Journal suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution: inspires follow-on research
rubrics_metrics.description: An important factor in evaluating a paper is the degree to which it will inspire follow-on research and propel the field forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to work that opens new directions; strike a balance between novelty and academic grounding. Favor papers likely to stimulate further research even if they are not perfectly polished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to nontraditional contribution types
rubrics_metrics.description: Value contributions that do not fit common SIGGRAPH paper patterns, including systems papers, experimental studies, novel datasets/benchmarks, and analysis of existing techniques/problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess these contributions on their potential to inspire follow-on work and move the field forward; do not dismiss because they lack a typical algorithmic novelty form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical soundness
rubrics_metrics.description: Each accepted paper should be technically sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure methods, experiments, analyses, claims, and conclusions are supported; technical flaws that affect correctness or validity are grounds for rejection, whereas minor fixable issues are not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepted papers must make a substantial contribution to computer graphics and interactive techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the significance and novelty of the contribution as part of the overall recommendation; consider whether the work advances the state of the art meaningfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor flaws should not cause rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor flaws can be corrected and should not be a reason to reject a paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between fixable/polishable issues and fundamental problems; allow the Conference track to accommodate less polished but novel ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific and thorough in reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews must be specific and detailed; vague statements like “this is well known” are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite specific publications or public disclosures when discussing related work; if you cannot find references, consider the possibility the contribution is novel. The explanation section is one of the most important parts of the review and often more important than the score—provide clear strengths, weaknesses, and actionable feedback for authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review scores and scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the scale: Strong Reject, Reject, Borderline Reject, Borderline Accept, Accept, and Strong Accept to evaluate each paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the contribution as a whole, including all aspects of the paper. For dual-track submissions, you may recommend Journal or Conference; the committee makes the final track decision. Interpret uniformly strong scores for dual-track submissions as indication for Journal acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete reviews by the stated deadline (2 March 2026).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to deadlines so authors can see full reviews before rebuttal; if you cannot meet the standard of a high-quality review or the deadline, return the paper early so a replacement can be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and double-blind reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: SIGGRAPH uses double-blind reviewing; authors must hide identities and follow the Anonymity Policy. Reviewers must not try to discover authors' identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ignore URLs in submissions unless absolutely necessary for review. Authors may include anonymized code/data repos with verifiable timestamps before the deadline; report any policy violations that reveal authors unless discovery timing precludes fair review. If you have concerns about originality, contact Technical Papers admin rather than pursuing identity discovery yourself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling prior and concurrent (non-peer-reviewed) work
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers are expected to compare to relevant published peer-reviewed work, but recent non-peer-reviewed preprints (e.g., arXiv) and newly published works should not be allowed to negatively affect the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not penalize authors for not citing non-peer-reviewed or very recent concurrent preprints. Authors are allowed, but not required, to cite concurrent preprints; if uncited, conditional acceptances can ask authors to add citations in revisions. Be mindful that authors may be unaware of rapidly posted online reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness of comparison requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons are important but should not require unnecessary or excessive work from authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the value of additional comparisons (e.g., perceptual studies or extensive method adaptations) against the burden and likelihood of affecting evaluation. Do not request comparisons to non-trivial-to-implement, hypothetical, or only loosely-related approaches; suggest follow-up papers for alternative approaches if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental comparisons must use publicly available code/data
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental comparisons can be required only to publicly available code/data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When requesting comparisons, provide public links to code/data for the work to compare to. If public code/data is not available, do not expect authors to implement it unless it is a minor change to an already implemented method (with available code), and limit requests to discussion otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource appropriateness for requested comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Required resources for a comparison should not exceed those of a typical lab or those already demonstrated in the submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests that require industrial-scale GPU clusters, unique measurement devices, or specialized high-end printers are inappropriate unless the paper itself already uses such resources; unreasonable resource demands harm inclusivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to review approved formats
rubrics_metrics.description: By accepting a paper for review you commit to review all materials submitted in approved formats: PDF for documents; MP4 for videos recommended; PNG or JPG for images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are unwilling to make this guarantee, recuse yourself. You are expected to make a reasonable effort to review materials in non-approved formats, but are not under the same absolute obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect ideas and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect the confidentiality of ideas in submissions: submissions are not public documents and may be considered proprietary by authors or employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not show the paper, videos, or other materials to anyone else unless they are explicitly helping with your review (see Review Process FAQ). Do not use ideas from papers you review to develop new work. Keep notes, marked manuscripts, videos, and implementations strictly confidential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflicts of interest and recuse promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid any situation that would create a conflict of interest; if assigned a paper that creates a possible conflict, return it immediately and do not submit a review. If a conflict is discovered after starting, recuse as soon as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include same institution as an author, direct involvement in the work, recent collaborations (past three years), advisor/advisee relationships (lifetime conflict), or having unpublished work that would be scooped by the submission. If recognition of authors could create perceived conflict, inform the senior reviewer or papers admin so reassignment can occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of LLMs in review
rubrics_metrics.description: Large language models (LLMs) are NOT allowed to be used for writing the reviews at any step, nor to share substantial content from the paper or your review with an LLM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may use LLMs for background research or to check short phrases for clarity. Grammar checker software that may have used LLMs is allowed. Do not ask an LLM to write content or translate substantive review content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be serious and provide substantive effort
rubrics_metrics.description: The review process is serious; provide solid, constructive reviews and avoid sketchy or flippant reviews that indicate insufficient reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are too busy or not competent to write a good review, return the paper early. Taking on too many reviews and failing to produce quality reviews is a significant problem. Treat reviews as important professional duties with career-impact implications for authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be professional and constructive
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid belittling or sarcastic comments or personal remarks; evaluate the work, not the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide respectful, carefully explained strengths and weaknesses and how you weigh them; the most valuable comments help authors understand shortcomings and how to improve their paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain reviewer anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: All reviewers are expected to maintain anonymity indefinitely and must not reveal themselves to authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not identify yourself to authors of accepted papers; requesting citations primarily to one’s own work may compromise anonymity and should be done with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of reviewer materials after review
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may be asked to review revised papers that were previously rejected and chose to release prior reviewers' names under a continuity process, so retaining notes or artifacts may be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you keep notes, marked manuscripts, videos, or implementations, keep them strictly confidential, insulate ideas learned from your own research and colleagues/students, and be aware that future reviewers may peruse your past reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide public links when requesting comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: When you request comparisons to prior work, include public links to the code/data for the work to compare to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enables authors to verify comparators and reduces undue burden; absence of public code/data generally means the comparison should be limited to discussion rather than new implementation.
